extracted.intended_audience: young people and parents (readers seeking guidance on manners, conduct, and child-rearing)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance on personal conduct, manners between the sexes, the moral training of children, and truthful speech aimed at cultivating gentlemanly/ladylike behavior and sound upbringing. Includes examples, anti-patterns, and practical reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid uncharitableness / speak kindly of others
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from saying evil of others; guard against thinking ill of persons and accustom the mind to look on the best side of persons and things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the 'Young Person' who labels a respectable boy 'no good' shows an odious habit. Practical guidance includes forming societies to repress unkind criticism and, when impossible to speak kindly, say nothing. Anti-pattern: quick, habitually negative judgments rooted in wounded vanity or neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard thoughts as well as speech
rubrics_metrics.description: To acquire the habit of saying no evil, it is advisable to guard against thinking it; put a guard upon the mind to accustom it to look on the best side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mental self-discipline is recommended—train to view people as not wholly bad. Example: refusing to indulge in internal harsh appraisals that lead to public unkindness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parents should model tolerance and charitable speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Older people, especially mothers, must set an example of tolerance and charitable speech because children reproduce their virtues and faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation used as encouragement: virtues of mothers are often visited upon the children. Practical: demonstrate tact, unselfishness, and tender charity so children copy them; form habits (e.g., a girls' pledge) to cultivate kindly speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer seats to women; gentlemanly unselfishness in public conveyances
rubrics_metrics.description: Men should give up seats to women on street-cars/trains regardless of how tired they are; doing so is an act of true gentlemanliness and humane consideration for women's comparative physical weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not weigh a woman's fashion, class, or attractiveness when offering a seat—'She is a woman! That should be sufficient.' Example contrast: foreign day-laborer gives his seat and is superior to a millionaire who hides behind a newspaper. Anti-pattern: refusing to rise out of pique or because one was not thanked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain deference despite others' discourtesy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not copy discourteous acts even if women or others behave rudely; two wrongs do not make a right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a woman laughs, whispers, or stares, that is rudeness but should not justify abandoning deference. Analogy: you do not adopt a drunkard's language because he is profane. Keep moral high ground and courtesy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid loudness in public speech and laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Public loud talking, constant laughing, and shrill voices (the 'loud' American girl) are defects in manners and indications of being ill-bred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare to softer-spoken national stereotypes (German Gretchen, Irish Bridget) and the peacock analogy: graceful appearance spoiled by a piercing call. Anti-pattern: being 'prononcée' in public conveyances and passing comments about fellow-passengers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge courtesies with gratitude
rubrics_metrics.description: When a man rises and offers his place, a woman should thank him; accepting as a matter of course is neglect of civility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the recipient doesn't thank, the giver should console himself by knowing he acted rightly. Avoid cynical reactions like 'Catch me giving a woman my seat again!'—persist in courteous behavior regardless of immediate recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe small courtesies that mark a gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple acts—raising the hat entirely from the head on meeting a woman, lifting it when she bows, rising when a woman enters a room, giving precedence in passing through doors, picking up a dropped handkerchief or glove—are sure indices of gentlemanliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These little attentions distinguish a true gentleman from a boor. Practice them habitually so they become instinctive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Girls should show deference to elders and avoid patronizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Young women must avoid a patronizing, superior air toward those older than themselves and should show the deference due to elders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temptation to tolerate or patronize elders is common; achieving discretion will remove foolish youthful manners. Practical: cultivate humility and respectful comportment in mixed-age social settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid brusqueness, pertness, and sarcastic mockery
rubrics_metrics.description: Brusqueness and pertness are not wit; selecting a courteous boy as a butt of sarcasm is shameful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such behavior is a common fault among girls aged fifteen to eighteen; it is a social misstep that will wear off with maturity. Anti-pattern: treating teasing as cleverness rather than unkindness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not spoil children; avoid over-indulgence
rubrics_metrics.description: Indulging a child—allowing him to have his own way—produces a stunted, warped, selfish character and is unjust both to the child and the parent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: physical frailty and early death among undisciplined children; long-term moral and physical consequences (delicate constitutions, early mortality). Parents should weigh whether indulgence is worth the likely harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforce implicit obedience and consistent discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The prime rule in training children should be implicit obedience: when a command or prohibition is stated there should be no appeal and coaxing must not avail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uncertainty and lack of consistent enforcement produce trying behavior; instances include inability to give medicine leading to death. Practical: line-upon-line, protest-upon-protest enforcement rather than 'letting alone.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider heredity and family health when deciding indulgence
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents should consider the stock on both sides of the family—if the physical constitution or family health is poor, neglect or over-indulgence may have especially harmful effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: children from ostensibly 'good stock' still suffered and some died when indulged; parental responsibility includes attending to physical wellbeing as well as moral training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not entrust discipline to untrained servants
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaving young children to servants whose wills and tempers are uncontrolled fosters insubordination because the child learns the nurse cannot insist on obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice: caregivers must be trained and empowered to enforce rules consistently; otherwise the child becomes a small tyrant with no respect for authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training should instill moral courage, self-denial, and submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective upbringing produces moral courage, self-denial, and the habit of submission so children can resist life's temptations and bear trials lightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for balanced character: young yet strong; spirited yet gentle; patient yet resolute. The author attributes personal lifelong benefits to such early training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace aging: remain active, useful, and engaged
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid dread of getting along in years; keep heart and soul young by constant occupation and unselfish interest in the affairs of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt juvenile dress or kittenish ways; instead beautify old age by steady usefulness. Example: a woman past fifty who shares young people's enjoyments and sympathy is praised. Anti-pattern: withdrawing to the chimney-corner and claiming one's place in the past.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not try to hide age by artificial means; cultivate natural ripeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid concealing age or imitating youth artificially; maturity is nearer perfection than crude youth and should be valued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor: the sun-and-frost-kissed Catawba grape is better than the tiny green sphere of June. Move the cultural 'dead-line' of old age forward by living fully and maintaining usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify facts before repeating; avoid spreading rumors
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious with secondhand information; do not allow ignorance of particulars to be filled by imagination and lead to false or sensational tales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: a girl's garbled account of a nurse administering 'ten grains of morphine' instead of the true mistake (two morphine powders given instead of doubling quinine) shows how snippets and imagination produce exaggeration. Principle: check facts before telling a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish truthfulness from impertinent frankness
rubrics_metrics.description: Being 'too frank'—uttering unnecessary and unkind criticism—is not the same as truthfulness; gratuitous honesty can be impertinent and insolent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a 'frank friend' who criticizes personal matters (gown fit, hair, household management) takes an unwarrantable liberty often rooted in captious temper. One may be entirely truthful without bestowing gratuitous advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exaggeration and sensationalism for attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not embellish or exaggerate stories to arouse attention; the temptation to 'let the truth spoil a good story' corrupts veracity and taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation for embellishment often arises from desire to be first or to entertain; such exaggeration produces 'impressionist-picture' romances of glare and abnormal perspective that vitiate symmetry and right coloring. Cultivate restraint and accuracy in narration.
